messages.subject: Re: Questions about year effects and dependent estimate
parts:
Hi Matt, list,

Apologies for my posting of earlier today -- hit the wrong button and sent to
the list before I'd finished the message. Here's a more complete version:
Here's my take on it; others may have different opinions.

Let's start by thinking about how you might go about answering your questions if
you were doing plot sampling -- ie were counting all birds within your points --
rather than distance sampling. Then you have a standard nested experimental
design, with visits within years within points within sites within treatments.
Your first question was about a treatment effect. To answer this you need to
decide what you're going to treat as a random effect and what you're treating
as a fixed effect. Any basic stats book or course will deal with this. For
example, if you're treating sites as random, you can then collapse all the
other stuff below that and your basic data are the density estimates per site;
you have a standard 2-way ANOVA-type setup with 4 treatments and 3 replicates
(sites) in each treatment. To answer your habitat questions, you want density
by site (so pool everything below that), and then you'd do a regression-type
model with covariates for habitat and probably site and treatment.

Things get a bit more complex when we introduce distance sampling, becuase as
you rightly said, one usually doesn't have enough samples to estimate a
separate detection function by site (first question above) or plot (second
question above). Instead, one usually uses the MCDS engine to fit covariates
to a global detection function, and then estimate detection function and
density by site (first question) or plot (second question) (for how to do this
in Distance, see Chapter 9 of the online manual, Estimating the detection
function at multiple levels). One could also try things like a completely
stratified detection function stratified by treatment, with covariates for
habitat, etc within each treatment (if sample size is large enough for a
separate detection function in each treatment), and use AIC to tell whether
this is better than an analysis without the detection function strata. In any
case, unless you estimate a separate detection function by site (first
question) or plot( second question) the estimates of h(0) for each site or plot
will not be independent of one another. This means that simple regression
methods such as those outlined above are not strictly valid as they assume each
density estimate is independent.

There are several potential solutions to this problem:
(i) ignore it, on the basis that it won't have too bad an effect on inference.
If you ignore the problem, you will tend to select too complex a regression
model using AIC, as the analysis will think there are more independent data
points (densities) than there really are; you will also tend to get too narrow
a variance estimate for the same reason.
(ii) use a resampling approach to get at the difference between treatments --
this will get around the too narrow variance problem. For example, define
delta12 as the mean difference in density between sites in treatment 1 and
treatment 2 from your data. To get a resampling based confidence interval on
this difference, you resample the data (e.g., resample the plots with
replacement, or the sites, depending on what is the random effect) refit the
detection functions and calculate new density estimats and then calculate a new
delta12, repeat this process many times and this gives you a distribution of
delta12s which you can use to get confidence intervals. This can easily be
generalized to getting paired differences between 4 treatments, etc. I think
Robin Russell, who has posted to this list before, has been using this kind of
approach with similar data to yours so you can ask her for details (search the
list archives for her contact info). Since you're estimating a detection
function lots of times using the resampled data, you'll likely want to do this
outside of the Distance GUI, by calling the analysis engines directly -- I've
previously posted stuff on this, and there's now an appendix in the Distance 5
manual about how to do this.
(iii) potentially use the same kind of approach in the habitat regression
question.

The above (ii) and (iii) don't solve the non-independence related model
selection problem - I don't have any thoughts on how to address this, but I
think it's a minor issue.

You asked about inverse variance weighting the estimates of point density in the
regression modelling -- you could do this if you like (can get variance
estimates for density by point from Distance) -- should increase precision in
theory, but you still have the non-independence problem. (I would use inverse
variance not inverse CV myself - not sure why 1/CV was suggested to you.)

You also asked about year effects. Then you want an estimate of density by
point for each year, and you'd include year in your regression model. If
bootstrapping by point, you want to make sure that if you select a point in
year 1 in a resample you also select the same point in year 2. Perhaps you
meant including year as a covariate in the detection function, in which case it
doesn't matter what layer you include it in within Distance -- all covariates
apply to the observation relevant to them (i.e., detection function modelling
takes place at the level of the observation).

A minor last point: you referred to your data collection method as a "point
count", whenmost people who collect distance data from points call it "point
transects" or "variable circular plots". Point count is the usual term for the
approach where you don't collect distances and end up with a relative index of
abundance.

Hope this makes sense -- typing in a bit of a rush. Feel free to email back
with further questions (although I might be a bit slow in responding).

- Len
